Benjamin Franklin, often regarded as one of America's founding fathers, was a prolific inventor, diplomat, and a prominent figure in the American Revolution. Born on January 11, 1779, in New York City, Franklin was born into a family of modest means but was raised with a strong sense of education and self-improvement.

Franklin's early years were spent in the small town of New York, where he was a naturalist and a self-proclaimed "fireman" who fixed fires and helped with the town's infrastructure. He was also a passionate advocate for education, often tutoring young men and women in mathematics, science, and literature. His work on the American colonies' independence from Britain was also a significant part of his life's work.

In 1794, Franklin became the first President of the United States' Committee on the Exeter House, a position he held for 13 years. During this time, he was instrumental in the development of the American colonies' foreign policy and was involved in the founding of the University of Pennsylvania.
